title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
directAnswer: To list every prime up to n, don't test each number for primality — instead cross out multiples. Keep a boolean array `isPrime[0..n]`, and for each prime p starting at 2, mark p's multiples as composite. The two tricks that make it fast: only loop p while p*p ≤ n, and start crossing out from p*p (not 2*p), because every smaller multiple of p was already crossed out by a smaller prime. Total work is O(n log log n).

remember.pattern: Cross out multiples instead of testing primality
rules: Start the inner crossing-out at **p*p**, not 2*p — every multiple of p below p*p already got crossed out by a smaller prime factor.
Stop the outer loop once **p*p > n**. Beyond that, any remaining unmarked number is prime; there is nothing left to cross out.
Initialise `isPrime[0] = isPrime[1] = false` — 0 and 1 are not prime, and forgetting this is the most common bug.
Use `p*p` as a `long` (or guard the loop) when n is large, so `p*p` doesn't overflow a 32-bit int.
It's O(n log log n) time and O(n) space — near-linear, far better than testing each of n numbers in O(√n).

You'll do many primality queries over a fixed range → precompute once, answer in O(1)
You need smallest-prime-factor or a multiplicative function (totient, Möbius) over a range
n is up to ~10⁷–10⁸ and fits in memory as a boolean array

The number is huge (hundreds of digits) → use Miller–Rabin, not a sieve
The range bound n is astronomically large → segmented sieve or a different approach
You need primes in a high window [L, R] with large L → segmented sieve, not the plain one
remember.takeaway: The sieve flips primality on its head: instead of asking 'is this number prime?' n times, it declares every number prime and lets each prime erase its own multiples. Starting at p*p and stopping at √n are the two optimisations that turn a naive O(n √n) idea into the near-linear O(n log log n) workhorse behind totient sieves, smallest-prime-factor tables, and fast factorisation.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know the sieve and can justify its two non-obvious optimisations — starting the inner loop at p*p and stopping the outer loop at √n — rather than reciting the loop bounds from memory.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Starting the inner loop at 2*p (correct but slower), running the outer loop all the way to n (wasted passes), or forgetting to mark 0 and 1 as non-prime.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain WHY p*p is the right start (smaller multiples already crossed out by smaller primes) and state the O(n log log n) bound, mentioning it comes from the sum of 1/p over primes ≤ n.

problemStatement:
Given an integer `n`, return all prime numbers in the range `[2, n]` in increasing order.

A **prime** is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself.

A closely related framing asks only for the **count** of primes strictly less than `n` (LeetCode 204, *Count Primes*) — the algorithm is identical; you just tally the survivors instead of collecting them.
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 5 × 10⁶ (typical interview bound; sieve memory is O(n))
n may be 0 or 1 → return an empty list (no primes)
understanding: We need every prime up to n, not a single yes/no test. Testing each number independently repeats a lot of work. The sieve instead records which numbers are still 'possibly prime', then walks the primes in order and erases their multiples. Whatever boolean is still set true at the end is prime, because no smaller prime ever divided it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we need the primes themselves, or just how many there are?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Either — the sieve is the same. Collect the survivors for the list, or count them for *Count Primes* (LeetCode 204).

clarifyingQuestions.question: What's the upper bound on n, and does the boolean array fit in memory?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A boolean[] of size n+1 is about n bytes in Java. For n = 5×10⁶ that's ~5 MB — fine. If n were 10⁹ you'd need a segmented sieve.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the range inclusive of n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll return primes in [2, n] inclusive. Count Primes uses a strict upper bound (< n) — I'll confirm which the prompt wants and adjust the final loop.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How should n = 0 or n = 1 behave?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Return an empty list. There are no primes ≤ 1.

approaches.name: Trial Division Per Number (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention first to anchor the cost you're improving on — it's the obvious 'test each number' idea.
hints: The dictionary definition of prime gives a direct test: a number x is prime if nothing in [2, x−1] divides it. How would you turn that into code for every number up to n?
You don't need to test divisors up to x−1 — if x = a*b then one of a, b is ≤ √x, so testing divisors up to √x suffices.
Wrap that √x primality test in a loop over every x from 2 to n. That's n tests, each up to √n work.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of the n numbers we try divisors up to √x ≤ √n, so the total is about n·√n. No array needed beyond the output, hence O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal reading of 'find all primes' is: for each number from 2 to n, run a primality test and keep it if it passes. The standard test asks whether any integer in [2, √x] divides x — if none does, x is prime.

**Why √x is enough for one test.** If x is composite, it factors as x = a·b with a ≤ b. Then a·a ≤ a·b = x, so a ≤ √x. Every composite therefore has a divisor at or below √x, so finding none up to √x proves x is prime. This already beats the naive 'test up to x−1' check.

**Why this still loses to the sieve.** We pay the √x test once per number, with no sharing of work between numbers. The number 90 gets tested for divisibility by 2, then 91 gets tested from scratch, then 92, and so on — even though 'is it even?' was answered a moment ago. The total climbs to roughly n·√n. For n = 10⁶ that's on the order of 10⁹ operations, noticeably slower than the sieve's ~10⁷.

**When it's actually the right call.** If you only need to test *one* number — 'is 1000003 prime?' — there's nothing to amortise and trial division to √x is the simplest correct answer. The sieve only wins when you want *all* primes up to n, so the crossing-out work is shared across the whole range.
approaches.insight: Trial division is correct and is the right tool for a single primality query. It loses for 'all primes up to n' purely because it shares no work between numbers — each test starts from zero. The sieve's whole advantage is that one prime's crossing-out pass benefits the entire range at once.

approaches.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want for 'all primes up to n'. Phrase it as 'each prime erases its own multiples' and justify the p*p start.
hints: Instead of asking 'is x prime?' for every x, flip it: assume everything is prime, then let each prime delete the numbers it divides. What's left undeleted must be prime.
Walk p from 2 upward. When you reach a p that's still marked prime, cross out p's multiples. Why can you stop increasing p once p*p > n?
When crossing out p's multiples, you can start at p*p instead of 2*p — every multiple of p smaller than p*p has a smaller prime factor and was already crossed out.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each prime p does about n/p crossing-out steps. Summing n/p over all primes p ≤ n gives n · Σ(1/p), and Σ(1/p) over primes ≤ n grows like log log n (Mertens' theorem). So the total is O(n log log n). The boolean array is O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Allocate `isPrime[0..n]`, set everything true, then mark 0 and 1 false. Sweep p from 2 upward. Whenever `isPrime[p]` is still true, p is genuinely prime — so cross out all of its multiples as composite. At the end, every index still marked true is prime.

**Why p must be prime when we reach it.** We process p in increasing order. If p had a smaller prime factor q < p, then when we processed q we already crossed out all multiples of q — including p itself. So the only way `isPrime[p]` is still true when we arrive is that p has no smaller prime factor, i.e. p is prime. That is the correctness backbone: the sieve never crosses out a prime, and it crosses out every composite (since every composite has at least one prime factor ≤ its square root that will reach it).

**Why crossing-out starts at p*p, not 2*p.** Consider the multiples of p: 2p, 3p, 4p, …, up to (p−1)p, p·p, …. Every multiple kp with k < p has a factor k that is smaller than p, and that smaller factor's smallest prime divisor is itself ≤ k < p — meaning kp was already crossed out during an earlier prime's pass. The first multiple of p that no smaller prime has touched is p·p. Starting there skips a pile of redundant writes and is a pure optimisation, not a correctness requirement.

**Why the outer loop stops at √n.** If p > √n, then p·p > n, so there is no multiple of p in range left to cross out — the inner loop body would never execute. Any index above √n that is still marked true at that point is simply prime and needs no further work. Stopping the outer loop at p·p ≤ n avoids pointless iterations.

**Why the time is O(n log log n).** Prime p crosses out roughly n/p numbers. The total writes are n/2 + n/3 + n/5 + n/7 + … over primes ≤ n, which is n times the sum of reciprocals of primes. That prime-reciprocal sum grows like log log n — astonishingly slowly — so the whole sieve is near-linear. This is why the sieve crushes the O(n √n) trial-division approach.
approaches.insight: The sieve's speed comes from sharing work: one pass for prime p benefits the entire range, and the start-at-p*p trick means each composite is crossed out only by its prime factors that haven't appeared yet. The deep fact behind O(n log log n) is that primes thin out fast enough that Σ(1/p) barely grows — the harmonic-like sum over primes is log log n, not log n.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Crossing out from 2*p instead of p*p
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Every multiple of p below p*p (namely 2p, 3p, …, (p−1)p) has a factor smaller than p, so it was already crossed out by a smaller prime. Starting at 2*p repeats all that work — correct, just slower.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Running the outer loop to n
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Once p > √n, p*p > n and there is no multiple of p left in range — the inner loop never executes, so iterating p up to n is pure waste.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting 0 and 1 are not prime
commonMistakesDetailed.why: An all-true initial array leaves indices 0 and 1 marked prime; they are never crossed out, so they wrongly appear in the result.

patternNote: Canonical Sieve over a range. Reach for it whenever you need a multiplicative or primality property for ALL values up to n, not a single query. The same cross-out skeleton powers the totient sieve, the Möbius sieve, and smallest-prime-factor tables.
